Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed (I.I.D) normal random variables, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then 

$$
Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}∼N(n\mu ,\,n{\sigma }^{2}).
$$

Therefore, since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{14}$ are independent and identically distributed, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{14} & ∼N(14\cdot 5,\,14\cdot {2}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(14\cdot 5,\,14\cdot 4) \\  & =N(70,56).\end{aligned}
$$

We wish to compute the probability $P(70\le Y\le 78).$ We first convert $Y$ into a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(70\le Y\le 78) & =P(\frac{70-70}{\sqrt{56}}\le Z\le \frac{78-70}{\sqrt{56}}) \\  & =P(0\le Z\le \frac{8}{\sqrt{56}}) \\  & =P(0\le Z\le 1.07) \\  & =Φ(1.07)-Φ(0) \\  & =Φ(1.07)-0.5\end{aligned}
$$

From the $z$-table, we have

$$
Φ(1.07)=0.8577.
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(70\le Y\le 78)=Φ(1.07)-0.5=0.8577-0.5=0.3577.
$$

$$

$$
P(16\le Y\le 20)=2Φ(0.67)-1=0.4972.

questions.problem:
A sports shop sells table tennis balls in boxes of $6.$ The weight of a table tennis ball, in grams, is normally distributed with a mean of $2.72\,\text{g}$ and a standard deviation of $0.05\,\text{g},$ while the weight of a box, in grams, is normally distributed with a mean of $12\,\text{g}$ and a standard deviation of $2\,\text{g}.$ If one box full of balls is randomly selected, what is the probability that it weighs less than $30\,\text{g}?$
You may assume that the weights are mutually independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*

| $z$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.7\,$ | $\,0.7611\,$ | $\,0.7642\,$ | $\,0.7673\,$ | $\,0.7704\,$ |
| $\,0.8\,$ | $\,0.7910\,$ | $\,0.7939\,$ | $\,0.7967\,$ | $\,0.7995\,$ |
| $\,0.9\,$ | $\,0.8186\,$ | $\,0.8212\,$ | $\,0.8238\,$ | $\,0.8264\,$ |
questions.worked_solution:
Let ${X}_{i}$ denote the weight of the $i$th ball, and let $Y$ denote the weight of a box. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(2.72,{0.05}^{2}),\,1\le i\le 6,
$$

and

$$
Y∼N(12,{2}^{2}).
$$

Let the random variable $W$ denote the weight of a randomly selected box of balls. Then, since

$$
W={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{6}+Y,
$$

we have that $W$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[W] & =6\cdot 2.72+12 \\  & =28.32 \\ \text{Var}[W] & =6\cdot {0.05}^{2}+{2}^{2} \\  & =4.015.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
W∼N(28.32,4.015).
$$

In order to find $P(W<30),$ we convert $W$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W<30) & =P(Z<\frac{30-28.32}{\sqrt{4.015}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<0.84) \\  & =Φ(0.84)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(0.84)≈0.7995.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W<30) & ≈Φ(0.84) \\  & ≈0.7995.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
A math test is composed of $15$ exercises. The time that a student takes to solve an exercise, in minutes, is normally distributed with a mean of $6\,\text{min}$ and a standard deviation of $2\,\text{min}.$ If one student is randomly selected, what is the probability that they will take between $80\,\text{min}$ and $100\,\text{min}$ to complete all exercises? You may assume that the times spent solving each exercise are mutually independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ | $\,0.09\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,1.0\,$ | $\,0.8554\,$ | $\,0.8577\,$ | $\,0.8599\,$ | $\,0.8621\,$ |
| $\,1.1\,$ | $\,0.8770\,$ | $\,0.8790\,$ | $\,0.8810\,$ | $\,0.8830\,$ |
| $\,1.2\,$ | $\,0.8962\,$ | $\,0.8980\,$ | $\,0.8997\,$ | $\,0.9015\,$ |
questions.worked_solution:
Let ${X}_{i}$ denote the time spent solving the $i$th exercise. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(60,{2}^{2}),\,1\le i\le 15.
$$

Let the random variable $W$ denote the time it takes a randomly selected student to complete the test. Then, since

$$
W={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{15},
$$

we have that $W$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[W] & =15\cdot 6 \\  & =90, \\ \text{Var}[W] & =15\cdot {2}^{2} \\  & =60.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
W∼N(90,60).
$$

In order to find $P(80<W<100),$ we convert $W$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(80<W<100) & =P(\frac{80-90}{\sqrt{60}}<Z<\frac{100-90}{\sqrt{60}}) \\  & ≈P(-1.29<Z<1.29) \\  & =Φ(1.29)-Φ(-1.29) \\  & =Φ(1.29)-(1-Φ(1.29)) \\  & =2Φ(1.29)-1\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(1.29)≈0.9015.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(80<W<100) & ≈2Φ(1.29)-1 \\  & ≈0.8030.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(70,{5}^{2}),\,1\le i\le 20.
$$

Let the random variable $W$ denote the weight of a randomly selected bouquet. Then, since

$$
W={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{20},
$$

we have that $W$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[W] & =20\cdot 70 \\  & =1\,400, \\ \text{Var}[W] & =20\cdot {5}^{2} \\  & =500.\end{aligned}

Therefore,

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W>1\,430) & =P(Z>\frac{1\,430-1\,400}{\sqrt{500}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>1.34) \\  & =1-P(Z<1.34) \\  & =1-Φ(1.34)\end{aligned}

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(1.34)≈0.9099.

$$

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ |

$$

and

$$

$$

$$
W={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{12}+Y,
$$

we have that $W$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[W] & =12\cdot 65+50 \\  & =830, \\ \text{Var}[W] & =12\cdot {5}^{2}+{2}^{2} \\  & =304.\end{aligned}

$$
W∼N(830,304).

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W>850) & =P(Z>\frac{850-830}{\sqrt{304}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>1.15) \\  & =1-P(Z<1.15) \\  & =1-Φ(1.15)\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Calculating Distributions and Probabilities With I.I.D Normal Random Variables
canonical_examples.problem:
Given that $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{6}$ are I.I.D random variables, where

$$
X_i \sim N(2,3^2), \qquad 1\leq i \leq 6,
$$

calculate $P(10\leq Y\leq 14),$ where  $Y = X_1+X_2+\cdots + X_{6}.$

*Hint: A table of values of $\Phi(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $\Phi(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\, 0.06 \,$ | $\, 0.07 \,$ | $\, 0.08 \,$ | $\, 0.09 \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\, 0.2 \,$ | $\, 0.6026 \,$ | $\, 0.6064 \,$ | $\, 0.6103 \,$ | $\, 0.6141 \,$ |
| $\, 0.3 \,$ | $\, 0.6406 \,$ | $\, 0.6443 \,$ | $\, 0.6480 \,$ | $\, 0.6517 \,$ |
| $\, 0.4 \,$ | $\, 0.6772 \,$ | $\, 0.6808 \,$ | $\, 0.6844 \,$ | $\, 0.6879 \,$ |
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed (I.I.D) normal random variables, where 

$$
X_i \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2), \qquad 1\leq i \leq n,
$$

then 

$$
Y = X_1+X_2+\cdots + X_n\sim N(n\mu, \: n\sigma^2).
$$

Therefore, since $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{6}$ are independent and identically distributed, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{6} & ∼N(6\cdot 2,\,6\cdot {3}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(6\cdot 2,\,6\cdot 9) \\  & =N(12,54).\end{aligned}
$$

We wish to compute the probability $P(10\leq Y \leq 14).$ We first convert $Y$ into a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(10\le Y\le 14) & =P(\frac{10-12}{\sqrt{54}}\le Z\le \frac{14-12}{\sqrt{54}}) \\  & =P(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{54}}\le Z\le \frac{2}{\sqrt{54}}) \\  & =P(-0.27\le Z\le 0.27) \\  & =Φ(0.27)-Φ(-0.27) \\  & =Φ(0.27)-(1-Φ(0.27)) \\  & =2Φ(0.27)-1\end{aligned}
$$

From the $z$-table, we have

$$
\Phi(0.27) = 0.6064.
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(10\leq Y \leq 14) = 2\Phi(0.27) - 1 = 0.2128.
$$

Example: 
                    Calculating Distributions and Probabilities With I.I.D Normal Random Variables In Context
canonical_examples.problem:
In a library, each shelf is filled with $20$ volumes of an encyclopedia, plus one bookend. The weight of one volume, in grams, is normally distributed with a mean of $150\,\textrm g$ and a standard deviation of $5\,\textrm g,$ while the weight of a bookend, in grams, is normally distributed with a mean of $50\,\textrm g$ and a standard deviation of $2\,\textrm g.$ If one shelf is randomly selected, what is the probability that it supports a weight of more than $3\,000\,\textrm g?$ You may assume that the weights of the volumes and bookend are mutually independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $\Phi(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $\Phi(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\, 0.00 \,$ | $\, 0.01 \,$ | $\, 0.02 \,$ | $\, 0.03 \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\, 2.0 \,$ | $\, 0.9772 \,$ | $\, 0.9778 \,$ | $\, 0.9783 \,$ | $\, 0.9788 \,$ |
| $\, 2.1 \,$ | $\, 0.9821 \,$ | $\, 0.9826 \,$ | $\, 0.9830 \,$ | $\, 0.9834 \,$ |
| $\, 2.2 \,$ | $\, 0.9861 \,$ | $\, 0.9864 \,$ | $\, 0.9868 \,$ | $\, 0.9871 \,$ |
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $X_i$ denote the weight of the $i$th volume, and let $Y$ denote the weight of a bookend. Then, we have

$$
X_i \sim N(150, 5^2), \qquad 1\leq i \leq 20,
$$

and

$$
Y \sim N(50, 2^2).
$$

Let the random variable $W$ denote the weight of a randomly selected shelf. Then, since

$$
W = X_1+X_2+\cdots + X_{20} + Y,
$$

we have that $W$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[W] & =20\cdot 150+50 \\  & =3\,050, \\ \text{Var}[W] & =20\cdot {5}^{2}+{2}^{2} \\  & =504.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
W \sim N(3\,050, 504).
$$

In order to find $P(W > 3\,000),$ we convert $W$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W>3\,000) & =P(Z>\frac{3\,000-3\,050}{\sqrt{504}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>-2.23) \\  & =P(Z<2.23) \\  & =Φ(2.23)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\Phi(2.23)\approx 0.9871.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W>3\,000) & ≈Φ(2.23) \\  & =0.9871.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
A set of random variables is said to be **independent and identically distributed** (or **I.I.D.**) if the random variables are mutually independent and have the same probability distribution.

When we conduct a random sample of size $n$ from a population, the sample elements

$$
X_1,\quad X_2,\quad \ldots,\quad X_n
$$

are often considered to be I.I.D. random variables. This assumption often allows us to simplify the statistical analysis. 

Suppose that the random variables $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ are I.I.D, where

$$
X_i\sim N(\mu, \sigma^2), \qquad 1\leq i \leq n.
$$

Let's consider their sum

$$
Y = X_1+X_2+\cdots + X_n.
$$

Since each $X_i$ is normally distributed, it follows that $Y$ is normally distributed as well. Moreover, we can compute the mean and the variance of $Y$ as follows:

- Calculating the mean using the properties of expectation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =\text{E}[{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}_{1}]+\text{E}[{X}_{2}]+⋯+\text{E}[{X}_{n}] \\  & =\mu +\mu +⋯+\mu  \\  & =n\mu .\end{aligned}
$$

- Similarly, using the properties of variance, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{Var}[{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}] \\  & =\text{Var}[{X}_{1}]+\text{Var}[{X}_{2}]+⋯+\text{Var}[{X}_{n}] \\  & ={\sigma }^{2}+{\sigma }^{2}+⋯+{\sigma }^{2} \\  & =n{\sigma }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
Y = X_1+X_2+\cdots+X_n\sim N(n\mu, n\sigma^2).
$$

We will soon use this important result to develop models of how random samples are distributed. But for now, let's practice working with I.I.D normal random variables.
